slides.0.title: Winemaking and Rosé Craft
slides.0.subtitle: Direct press, short maceration, saignée and colour control
slides.1.title: Three rosé methods
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Direct press
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Red grapes pressed immediately with minimal skin contact: pale, delicate, the Provençal signature
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Short maceration
slides.1.highlights.1.content: A brief soak on skins before pressing to gain colour and aroma
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Saignée
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Bleeding juice off a red fermentation; sources differ on whether it is allowed or discouraged, so it is not tested
slides.1.content: Method shapes colour and flavour.
slides.2.title: Protecting flavour
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Cold and inert gas
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Chilling fruit and press protects aromas and prevents oxidation and over-extraction
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Thiols and esters
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Early picking and cool fermentation preserve citrus-tropical thiols and fermentation esters
slides.2.highlights.2.title: No malolactic
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Malolactic fermentation is usually avoided to keep crisp acidity
slides.2.content: The goal is fresh, pure and pale.
slides.3.title: Colour and quality
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Colour is not quality
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Pale is a style choice, not a quality guarantee; deeper Bandol rosé can be equally fine
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Measuring colour
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Industry colorimeters and colour charts quantify colour to keep a consistent regional style
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Oak and ageing
slides.3.highlights.2.content: A few top rosés see oak and ageing, such as Bandol and some Palette
slides.3.content: Style is a choice; quality has its own measure.
